checkpoints: A persisted-query hash is only meaningful as a content identifier - the hash-to-query mapping is trustworthy only when the server itself proves hash equals SHA-256(query) at registration time, rather than accepting whatever pairing a client asserts.

In this implementation, the register endpoint calls `store.set(body.hash, body.query)` directly on unverified client input; because registration now happens outside Apollo's `persistedQueries.cache.set`, Apollo's own built-in hash-matches-query verification never runs at all.

Since the store never checks that the hash matches the query, any client can register an attacker-chosen query under a hash the legitimate app is already known to send hash-only, overwriting or seeding that exact cache entry.

Once a malicious pair is registered, every subsequent hash-only request from real clients - including the official app itself - resolves to and executes the attacker's query instead of the original one, turning a bandwidth optimization into a remote-injection primitive that redirects an entire population of well-behaved callers without touching their code.

The minimum fix is to recompute `sha256(query)` on every store write and reject the request (4xx) when it doesn't equal the supplied hash, which restores exactly the guarantee Apollo's built-in persisted-query cache already provides, making the custom register endpoint unnecessary in favor of the standard protocol.

A stronger posture removes client-driven registration entirely: a build-time trusted-documents allowlist generates the hash-to-query manifest from the client's real query set ahead of time, so the server only ever executes pre-approved hashes and never accepts a query string from a request.

The store backing this registry is an unbounded Map with no TTL or eviction, so junk registrations let it grow forever with no way to bound memory or age out stale entries, compounding the security risk with a resource-growth issue.

Correctness here is proven by tests showing a mismatched hash/query pair is rejected without altering the existing entry for that hash, a legitimate register-then-hash-only round trip still resolves, and repeated junk registrations cannot evict or replace a known-good mapping.

A batching data loader only collapses keys that get registered within the same event-loop tick (the batch dispatch window) into one call; once that window closes, any further `load()` calls open a new window of their own.

Awaiting a `load()` call inside a `for...of` loop fully pauses that iteration until the promise resolves, so the next iteration's `load()` call happens on a later tick — this closes the batch window after exactly one key every time, even though the loader's batch function and scope are configured correctly.

N single-key batch lines in the data-source log (`[BATCH] ... IN ('<one-id>')` repeated N times) instead of one combined multi-key line is the fingerprint of broken batching — it is N+1 in disguise, N sequential round-trips happening despite a batching loader being wired up.

The root cause lives in the calling code's control flow, not in the loader's configuration: the loader itself, its batch function, and its request scope are not the source of the bug, so 'fixing' the loader's setup would not resolve the slowdown.

The fix is to register every `load()` call before awaiting any of them, so all keys land in the same tick: mapping over the collection to start every `load()` synchronously and only then awaiting them together (e.g. with a single combined wait over all the pending calls) lets the loader batch them into one `IN (...)` query.

Turning the related field into its own field resolver that returns the loader's pending call directly, without an `await` inside that resolver, is the more idiomatic fix — the GraphQL engine itself invokes that field once per parent within the same execution tick, so all the resulting `load()` calls naturally land in the same batch window without any manual `Promise.all`.

The loader's per-request cache deduplicates a key that gets loaded twice within the same request, but that is a separate mechanism from batching by width; since every key in this scenario is unique, the cache cannot mask or fix a sequential-await bug like this one.

Proving the fix requires counting batch-log lines for the same nested query before and after (N single-key lines collapsing to one multi-key line) and re-measuring latency against the size of the parent list (linear growth flattening out), then locking in a regression test that asserts exactly one batch-log line per relation per request so the sequential-await bug cannot silently return.

APQ's payoff is amortisation: after a one-time round trip where the client registers the full query and receives a hash back, every subsequent call sends only a 64-character SHA-256 hash instead of the full query text.

That payoff only holds if a registered hash means something the whole fleet agrees on. `PersistedQueryStore.store` is a plain `Map` living in a single NestJS process's heap, so a hash set by one replica is invisible to the `Map` instances running in the other replicas.

With 4 replicas behind round-robin routing and no shared cache, a hash registered on one replica is recognized only when a later request happens to land back on that same replica - about 1 in 4 times - while the other 3 in 4 requests still return PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND. That is the arithmetic source of the observed ~75% miss rate.
A rolling restart clears the in-memory `Map` on whichever pod cycles, erasing every hash that pod had learned and forcing a fresh miss storm across the fleet as clients re-register from scratch.

The fix has to match the registry's storage to the unit of deployment (the whole fleet) rather than the unit of a single process. Apollo Server's `persistedQueries.cache` accepts any object implementing `get`/`set`/`delete`, so the storage backend is a drop-in swap that requires no resolver code changes.

Backing the registry with a shared store such as Redis (for example `apollo-server-cache-redis`'s `RedisCache`), combined with a TTL so the registry doesn't grow unbounded, makes a registration visible to every replica and lets it survive any single pod restarting.

For first-party clients, generating a hash-to-query manifest at build time and shipping it with the client (trusted documents) goes further: the server never accepts an arbitrary client-supplied registration at all, which removes both the miss storm and the open registration attack surface in one move.

Validating the fix requires more than reading the diff: the `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` rate should fall to near zero at steady state, average request payload should shrink to hash-size, a rolling-restart soak should confirm registrations survive pod churn, and the Redis-backed store itself should be load-tested so its added network hop doesn't become the new bottleneck.

DataLoader's batch function must return a result array of the exact same length and order as the keys array it receives, because DataLoader hands result[i] back to whichever caller invoked load(keys[i]) — matching happens purely by index, never by inspecting the content of the returned rows.

Grouping a flat SQL result set by iterating the rows themselves — rather than iterating the original keys array — produces an output ordered by whatever sequence the rows first appeared in, since an unordered SQL IN clause never guarantees it will return rows in the same order as the ids that were passed in.

An author with zero books contributes no group to a row-order-based grouping, so it doesn't just occupy the wrong slot itself — it silently deletes one array slot and shifts the position of every subsequent author's group by one index, compounding the misalignment for everything after it.

The batched query itself is correct and genuinely avoids N+1, which means this class of bug can hide behind SQL that looks completely fine — the defect lives entirely in how the batch function reshapes its query results back into the keys' order, not in the query.

The symptom is intermittent rather than constant because the misalignment only manifests when the database's row-return order diverges from the requested keys' order or a zero-books author sits among the batch; whenever the two orders happen to coincide, the mismatched code produces correct-looking output by coincidence.

A single-author query never exposes this bug because batching only ever contains one key, so there is nothing for that one result to be out of order relative to — it always lands at index 0 regardless of how the batch function grouped it, making single-key tests a red herring that masks the real defect.

The correct fix is to build an intermediate map keyed by each id while iterating the rows, then derive the final result by mapping over the original keys array and looking up each key in that map, falling back to an empty array for keys with no matching rows — this guarantees position i always corresponds to keys[i] and makes missing entries explicit instead of silently absent.

Verifying the fix requires asserting that every returned child record's foreign key matches its parent's id in a nested query, plus a regression fixture where an entity with zero related rows is sandwiched between two entities that do have rows, since that specific arrangement is what exposes an index shift.

`new PubSub()` from `graphql-subscriptions` creates an in-process object — `publish()` only reaches `asyncIterator`s that were instantiated inside the same running Node process, not across any process boundary.
On a single dev instance there is only one process, so the mutation's `publish` call and the subscription's `asyncIterator` are always the same object — every event is delivered with no exceptions.

Running the service as 3 replicas behind a load balancer means each replica boots its own copy of the service with its own private, unshared `PubSub` instance in memory — there are effectively three separate topics that happen to share the same string name.

A subscriber's WebSocket is a long-lived connection pinned to whichever replica accepted the upgrade, while each `createPost` mutation is a separate HTTP/WS request the load balancer is free to route to any replica independently.

An event reaches a given subscriber only when the replica that ran the mutation happens to be the same replica the subscriber's WebSocket is connected to; with 3 replicas and roughly uniform routing that coincidence happens about 1 in 3 times, exactly matching the reported symptom.

Sticky WebSocket sessions do not fix this bug: stickiness only pins the subscriber's connection to one replica, but does nothing to the mutation request, which remains a separate call the load balancer can still send to any replica.

The correct fix is to replace the in-memory `PubSub` with an adapter backed by an external shared bus — such as `graphql-redis-subscriptions`'s `RedisPubSub` — so that `publish` and every replica's `asyncIterator` all read from and write to the same external topic regardless of which replica handled the mutation.

The fix can be verified by running 2+ instances locally, opening a subscription against one instance while firing mutations against a different instance, and confirming every event still arrives exactly once with no duplicates once all replicas share the same external bus.
